_about: Hand-written descriptions for lymph nodes, bones, viscera, fascia, bursae and tendon sheaths without a Wikipedia text. See app/extra_content.py.

Anterior cells of ethmoid bone.description: Anterior ethmoidal air cells: the front group of the ethmoidal labyrinth, draining into the middle meatus via the ethmoidal infundibulum and semilunar hiatus. They include the agger nasi cell and are part of the ostiomeatal complex, whose obstruction underlies most chronic maxillary and frontal sinusitis. Only the thin lamina papyracea separates them from the orbit, so ethmoiditis can spread to cause orbital cellulitis.

Middle cells of ethmoid bone.description: Middle ethmoidal air cells, including the ethmoidal bulla, the largest and most constant cell. They drain into the middle meatus above or on the bulla and lie medial to the orbit, separated from it by the thin lamina papyracea.

Posterior cells of ethmoid bone.description: Posterior ethmoidal air cells, draining into the superior meatus. They lie close to the optic canal and sphenoid sinus; a posterior cell extending over the sphenoid (Onodi cell) can place the optic nerve at risk during endoscopic sinus surgery.

Accessory parotid gland.description: Detached piece of parotid tissue present in many people, lying on the masseter between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct, into which it drains by one or more small ducts. It can give rise to the same tumours as the main gland and presents as a cheek mass.

Left medial segment of liver (IV).description: Couinaud segment IV: the part of the functional left liver lying to the right of the falciform ligament and umbilical fissure, between them and the middle hepatic vein (Cantlie line), and in front of the caudate lobe. It is divided into IVa above and IVb below, and corresponds largely to the anatomical quadrate lobe. It is supplied by the left portal vein and left hepatic artery and drained into the middle and left hepatic veins.

Mucosa of nasal cavity.description:
Mucous membrane lining the nasal cavity. Most of it is respiratory mucosa - ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells over a highly vascular lamina propria with venous (erectile) plexuses over the conchae - which warms, humidifies and filters inspired air and moves mucus back to the pharynx. The roof and upper septum carry olfactory mucosa; the vestibule is lined by skin.
Its rich blood supply meets in Kiesselbach's plexus on the anterior septum, the usual site of nosebleeds.

Superior parathyroid gland.description:
The upper of the two pairs of parathyroid glands, derived from the fourth pharyngeal pouch. It lies fairly constantly on the posterior surface of the thyroid near the cricothyroid junction, at the level where the recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the larynx, usually supplied by the inferior thyroid artery.
Parathyroid glands secrete parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium; they must be preserved at thyroidectomy to avoid hypocalcaemia.

Left lobe of thymus.description: One of the two asymmetric lobes of the thymus, lying in the superior and anterior mediastinum behind the sternum. The thymus is where T lymphocytes mature and are selected; it is large in children and involutes into fat after puberty. Thymic tumours (thymoma) are associated with myasthenia gravis.

Right lobe of thymus.description: One of the two asymmetric lobes of the thymus, lying in the superior and anterior mediastinum behind the sternum, in front of the great vessels. Each lobe has an outer cortex packed with developing T cells and a medulla with Hassall corpuscles; the organ is prominent in infants (the sail sign on chest films) and involutes after puberty.

Anterior inferior jugular nodes.description: Deep cervical lymph nodes on the lower part of the internal jugular vein (level IV region). They receive lymph from higher deep cervical nodes, the thyroid, larynx and trachea and drain into the jugular trunk.

Inferior deep lateral cervical nodes.description: The lower deep cervical nodes along the internal jugular vein below the omohyoid (level IV), including the jugulo-omohyoid node that drains the tongue. They receive lymph from the upper deep cervical nodes and directly from the thyroid, larynx, trachea and oesophagus, and drain into the jugular trunk. The left supraclavicular (Virchow) node, near the end of the thoracic duct, can be the first sign of abdominal cancer.

Lateral superior jugular node.description: Upper deep cervical node lying along the lateral side of the internal jugular vein under sternocleidomastoid (level II region), draining the parotid, upper neck and pharynx toward the lower deep cervical nodes.

Superficial anterior cervical nodes.description: Small nodes along the anterior jugular vein in the front of the neck, draining the skin and superficial tissues of the anterior neck into the deep cervical nodes.

Superficial lateral cervical nodes.description: Nodes along the external jugular vein on the surface of sternocleidomastoid. They drain the skin of the lateral neck, the lower ear and the parotid region and pass lymph to the deep cervical nodes.

Infra-auricular nodes.description: Parotid lymph nodes below the ear, at the lower pole of the parotid gland, draining the auricle, parotid and adjacent scalp and face toward the upper deep cervical nodes.

Pre-auricular nodes.description: Superficial parotid nodes just in front of the tragus. They drain the lateral eyelids and conjunctiva, the temple, anterior auricle and external acoustic meatus; enlargement accompanies viral and chlamydial conjunctivitis.

Superficial parotid nodes.description: Nodes on the surface of the parotid gland under its fascia, draining the forehead, temple, lateral eyelids, auricle and external acoustic meatus into the deep cervical nodes. They are a common site of metastasis from skin cancers of the face and scalp.

Intraglandular parotid nodes.description: Lymph nodes lying within the substance of the parotid gland, around the retromandibular vein and branches of the facial nerve. They drain the gland, the middle ear, nasal cavity, palate and overlying skin, and their involvement by skin cancer may require parotidectomy.

Brachial nodes.description: The lateral (humeral) group of axillary lymph nodes, along the medial and posterior side of the axillary vein. They drain most of the upper limb (except lymph that follows the cephalic vein) and pass it to the central and apical axillary nodes.

Deep popliteal nodes.description: Nodes around the popliteal vessels in the fat of the popliteal fossa. They receive lymph from the small saphenous territory (lateral foot, back of leg), the deep leg and the knee joint, and drain along the femoral vessels to the deep inguinal nodes.

Anterior tibial node.description: Small inconstant node on the interosseous membrane along the anterior tibial vessels, draining deep structures of the anterior leg toward the popliteal nodes.

Posterior tibial node.description: Small inconstant node along the posterior tibial vessels, draining deep tissues of the posterior leg toward the popliteal nodes.

Fibular node.description: Small inconstant node along the fibular vessels, draining deep tissues of the lateral and posterior leg toward the popliteal nodes.

Inferior superficial inguinal nodes.description: The vertical group of superficial inguinal nodes, along the terminal great saphenous vein below the saphenous opening. They drain most of the superficial lymph of the lower limb and pass it through the saphenous opening to the deep inguinal and external iliac nodes.

Superolateral superficial inguinal nodes.description: Superficial inguinal nodes below the lateral part of the inguinal ligament, draining the skin of the lower lateral abdominal wall below the umbilicus, the buttock and the flank.

Superomedial superficial inguinal nodes.description: Superficial inguinal nodes below the medial part of the inguinal ligament. They drain the lower anterior abdominal wall, the external genitalia (but not the testes, which drain to para-aortic nodes), the perineum, the lower anal canal below the pectinate line and, via the round ligament, part of the uterus.

Proximal deep inguinal node.description: The highest deep inguinal node (node of Cloquet or Rosenmüller), in the femoral canal just below the inguinal ligament. It links the deep inguinal to the external iliac nodes; its enlargement can mimic a femoral hernia and it is sampled in groin dissection for melanoma or vulval cancer.

Intermediate deep inguinal node.description: Deep inguinal node medial to the femoral vein, within the femoral canal region, receiving lymph from the deep lower limb, the glans penis or clitoris and the superficial inguinal nodes.

Lateral lacunar node.description: External iliac lymph node lying at the vascular lacuna under the inguinal ligament, lateral to the external iliac artery. The lacunar nodes link the inguinal and external iliac chains.

Medial lacunar node.description: External iliac lymph node lying at the vascular lacuna under the inguinal ligament, medial to the external iliac vein, near the femoral ring; it receives lymph from the deep inguinal nodes.

Intermediate lacunar node.description: External iliac lymph node at the vascular lacuna between the external iliac artery and vein, linking the inguinal and external iliac nodes.

Lateral vesical nodes.description: Nodes beside the bladder along the lateral umbilical ligament, draining the bladder toward the internal and external iliac nodes; they are removed at radical cystectomy.

Pararectal nodes.description: Nodes in the mesorectum along the superior rectal vessels, draining the rectum. Their involvement by rectal cancer is removed en bloc with the mesorectum in total mesorectal excision; lymph then passes up along the inferior mesenteric chain.

Inferior tracheobronchial nodes.description: The subcarinal nodes, below the tracheal bifurcation. They receive lymph from both lungs (especially the lower lobes), the heart and oesophagus and drain to the superior tracheobronchial and paratracheal nodes. Enlargement widens the carinal angle and is sampled by EBUS or mediastinoscopy in lung cancer staging.

Superior tracheobronchial nodes.description: Nodes in the angle between the trachea and each main bronchus, receiving lymph from the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes and passing it to the paratracheal nodes and bronchomediastinal trunks. Lymph from the left lower lobe often crosses to the right.

Paratracheal thoracic nodes.description: Nodes along both sides of the thoracic trachea, receiving lymph from the tracheobronchial nodes, trachea and oesophagus and draining into the bronchomediastinal trunks. They are key stations in lung cancer staging (N2 if ipsilateral).

Lateral pericardial nodes.description: Small nodes beside the pericardium along the pericardiacophrenic vessels, draining the pericardium and diaphragm to the anterior mediastinal nodes.

Node of arch of azygos vein.description: Lymph node beside the arch of the azygos vein on the right side of the trachea, one of the right paratracheal/tracheobronchial nodes draining the right lung and oesophagus.

Node of ligamentum arteriosum.description: Anterior mediastinal node at the ligamentum arteriosum, in the aortopulmonary window, near the left recurrent laryngeal nerve. It drains the left upper lobe; its enlargement by lung cancer can compress the nerve and cause hoarseness.

Iliopectineal arch.description: Thickened band of iliac fascia running from the inguinal ligament to the iliopubic eminence. It divides the space under the inguinal ligament into a lateral muscular lacuna (iliopsoas, femoral nerve, lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) and a medial vascular lacuna (femoral artery, vein and the femoral canal).

Lateral femoral intermuscular septum.description: Strong septum from the deep surface of the fascia lata and iliotibial tract to the lateral lip of the linea aspera, separating the anterior (extensor) compartment from the posterior (flexor) compartment of the thigh. Vastus lateralis arises partly from it; it is the landmark followed in the lateral approach to the femur.

Medial femoral intermuscular septum.description: Septum from the fascia lata to the medial lip of the linea aspera, between vastus medialis in front and the adductors behind, separating the anterior from the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh.

Lateral intermuscular septum of arm.description: Septum from the deep fascia of the arm to the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus, separating the anterior (flexor) from the posterior (extensor) compartment. The radial nerve and profunda brachii artery pierce it in the lower third of the arm, where the nerve is tethered and vulnerable in humeral shaft fractures (Holstein-Lewis fracture).

Subdeltoid bursa.description: Large bursa between the deltoid and the capsule of the shoulder joint and rotator cuff, usually continuous with the subacromial bursa. It lets the cuff glide under the deltoid and acromion. Subacromial-subdeltoid bursitis accompanies impingement and rotator cuff disease; it is the space injected with steroid for shoulder pain.

Subcutaneous acromial bursa.description: Subcutaneous bursa over the acromion, reducing friction between skin and bone; it may become inflamed with repeated pressure (for example from carrying loads on the shoulder).

Coracobrachial bursa.description: Bursa between the coracoid process and the conjoined tendon of coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps, over the subscapularis tendon. It often communicates with the subacromial bursa.

Subtendinous bursa of infraspinatus musc.description: Small bursa between the tendon of infraspinatus and the posterior capsule of the shoulder joint; it may communicate with the joint cavity.

Subtendinous bursa of teres major muscle.description: Bursa between the tendon of teres major and the humerus at its insertion on the medial lip of the intertubercular groove.

Subtendinous bursa of trapezius muscle.description: Bursa between the ascending (lower) fibres of trapezius and the smooth triangular area at the medial end of the spine of the scapula.

Subtendinous bursa of triceps brachii mu.description: Deep bursa between the triceps tendon and the olecranon near its insertion, separate from the larger subcutaneous olecranon bursa.

Intertubercular tendon sheath.description: Synovial sheath surrounding the tendon of the long head of biceps as it runs in the intertubercular (bicipital) groove, an extension of the synovial membrane of the shoulder joint. It is inflamed in bicipital tenosynovitis, and a shoulder effusion can be seen around the tendon on ultrasound.

Common flexor tendon sheath.description:
The ulnar bursa: the synovial sheath enclosing the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus as they pass through the carpal tunnel, extending from above the flexor retinaculum to the mid-palm and continuing along the little finger's tendons in most people.
Infection of the little finger sheath can spread into it, and through the space of Parona to the thumb's sheath (radial bursa), producing a horseshoe abscess.

Synovial sheaths of digits of hand.description: Synovial sheaths that wrap the long flexor tendons in the fibrous digital sheaths of the fingers, from the metacarpal heads to the distal phalanges. Those of the index, middle and ring fingers are usually separate from the palmar sheaths. Infective flexor tenosynovitis gives Kanavel's four signs: a flexed finger, fusiform swelling, tenderness along the sheath and pain on passive extension.

Cruciform part of fibrous sheath of digi.description: The cruciate pulleys (C1-C3): thin, crossing fibres of the fibrous flexor sheath of the fingers, lying over the joints between the stronger annular pulleys. They let the sheath fold during flexion while keeping the tendons close to the bone.

Tendon sheath - abd. pollicis longus - e.description: Synovial sheath around the tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the first dorsal compartment of the wrist, over the radial styloid. Its thickening and inflammation cause De Quervain tenosynovitis, with pain on ulnar deviation of the wrist with the thumb held in the palm (Finkelstein test).

Tendon sheath of extensors carpi radiali.description: Synovial sheath of extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis in the second dorsal compartment of the wrist. Where these tendons are crossed by the first-compartment muscles a few centimetres above the wrist, friction causes intersection syndrome.

Tendon sheath of extensor pollicis longu.description: Synovial sheath of extensor pollicis longus in the third dorsal compartment, where the tendon turns around Lister's tubercle. The tendon may rupture here weeks after a distal radius fracture or in rheumatoid arthritis.

Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum and.description: Synovial sheath of the tendons of extensor digitorum and extensor indicis in the fourth dorsal compartment of the wrist; it is often involved by rheumatoid tenosynovitis.

Tendon sheath of extensor digiti minimi.description: Synovial sheath of extensor digiti minimi in the fifth dorsal compartment, over the distal radio-ulnar joint. Erosion of the ulnar head in rheumatoid arthritis can rupture this and the adjacent tendons (Vaughan-Jackson syndrome).

Tendon sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris.description: Synovial sheath of extensor carpi ulnaris in the sixth dorsal compartment, in the groove of the ulnar head. Its subsheath can tear, letting the tendon snap out of the groove in forearm rotation (ECU subluxation), a source of ulnar-sided wrist pain in racquet sports.

Tendon sheath of flexor carpi radialis.description: Synovial sheath of flexor carpi radialis in its own tunnel through the flexor retinaculum and the groove of the trapezium, separate from the carpal tunnel.

Tendon sheath of flexor pollicis longus.description: The radial bursa: synovial sheath of flexor pollicis longus through the carpal tunnel, continuous with its digital sheath to the distal phalanx of the thumb. It may connect with the ulnar bursa, letting infection spread between thumb and little finger.

Tendon sheath of tibialis anterior.description: Synovial sheath around the tendon of tibialis anterior under the superior and inferior extensor retinacula, in front of the ankle.

Tendon sheath of extensor hallucis longu.description: Synovial sheath around the tendon of extensor hallucis longus under the extensor retinacula on the front of the ankle.

Tendon sheath of extensor digitorum long.description: Synovial sheath shared by the tendons of extensor digitorum longus and fibularis tertius under the extensor retinacula on the front of the ankle.

Tendon sheath of tibialis posterior musc.description: Synovial sheath of tibialis posterior as it passes behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum, the most anterior tendon in the tarsal tunnel. Tenosynovitis and degeneration of this tendon lead to adult-acquired flatfoot.

Tendon sheath of flexor digitorum longus.description: Synovial sheath of flexor digitorum longus behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum, between the sheaths of tibialis posterior and flexor hallucis longus.

Tendon sheath of flexor hallucis longus.description: Synovial sheath of flexor hallucis longus as it runs in its groove on the back of the talus and under the sustentaculum tali. Tenosynovitis here is common in ballet dancers.

Common tendon sheath of fibularis muscle.description: Synovial sheath shared by fibularis longus and brevis behind the lateral malleolus, under the superior fibular retinaculum; it divides lower down into separate sheaths. Tearing of the retinaculum lets the tendons dislocate over the malleolus.

Plantar tendon sheath of fibularis longu.description: Synovial sheath of the fibularis longus tendon in the sole, where it runs in the groove of the cuboid and crosses the foot obliquely to the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal base.

Subtendinous bursa of tibialis anterior.description: Bursa between the tendon of tibialis anterior and the medial cuneiform near its insertion.

Subcutaneous bursa of medial malleolus.description: Subcutaneous bursa over the medial malleolus, which may become inflamed by pressure from footwear.

Subcutaneous bursa of lateral malleolus.description: Subcutaneous bursa over the lateral malleolus, which may become inflamed by pressure from footwear or sitting cross-legged.

Subcutaneous calcaneal bursa.description: Bursa between the skin and the Achilles tendon near the heel. Inflammation from tight heel counters produces a tender swelling (pump bump) at the back of the heel.

Subtendinous calcaneal bursa.description: The retrocalcaneal bursa, between the Achilles tendon and the upper part of the posterior surface of the calcaneus. It is inflamed in retrocalcaneal bursitis, often with a prominent posterosuperior calcaneus (Haglund deformity), and in seronegative spondyloarthritis.

Suprapatellar bursa.description: Large bursa between the quadriceps tendon and the front of the femur, extending about a hand's breadth above the patella. It communicates freely with the knee joint, so a knee effusion fills it and bulges above the patella; articularis genus holds it up during extension. It is the usual site for aspirating or injecting the knee.

Subcutaneous prepatellar bursa.description: Bursa between the skin and the front of the patella. Repeated kneeling inflames it (prepatellar bursitis, housemaid's knee), giving a fluctuant swelling in front of the patella; it can also become infected after skin abrasions.

Subfacial prepatellar bursa.description: Prepatellar bursa lying deep to the fascia over the patella, part of the multilayered prepatellar bursal system.

Subtendinous prepatellar bursa.description: Deepest prepatellar bursa, between the quadriceps tendon expansion and the patella.

Subcutaneous infrapatellar bursa.description: Bursa between the skin and the lower patellar ligament and tibial tuberosity. Inflammation from kneeling upright (clergyman's knee) produces swelling below the patella.

Deep infrapatellar bursa.description: Bursa between the patellar ligament and the upper tibia, below the infrapatellar fat pad; it lets the ligament glide over the bone.

Subcutaneous bursa of tuberosity of tibi.description: Bursa between the skin and the tibial tuberosity, commonly inflamed by kneeling.

Semimembranosus bursa.description: Bursa between the semimembranosus tendon and the medial tibial condyle and medial head of gastrocnemius. It often communicates with the knee joint; distension of this gastrocnemio-semimembranosus bursa by a knee effusion is a Baker (popliteal) cyst, which may rupture and mimic a deep vein thrombosis.

Medial subtendinous bursa of gastrocnemi.description: Bursa under the medial head of gastrocnemius near its origin on the femur, usually communicating with the knee joint and with the semimembranosus bursa - the anatomical basis of the Baker (popliteal) cyst.

Lateral subtendinous bursa of gastrocnem.description: Bursa beneath the lateral head of gastrocnemius near its femoral origin, occasionally communicating with the knee joint.

Superior bursa of biceps femoris muscle.description: Bursa near the origin of the long head of biceps femoris on the ischial tuberosity, separating it from the semimembranosus tendon.

Inferior subtendinous bursa of biceps fe.description: Bursa between the biceps femoris tendon and the lateral collateral ligament of the knee near their attachment to the fibular head.

Subtendinous bursa of sartorius muscle.description: Bursa between the tendon of sartorius and the tendons of gracilis and semitendinosus near the pes anserinus; together with the anserine bursa it is inflamed in pes anserine bursitis, with pain on the medial upper tibia.

Subtendinous bursa of iliacus muscle.description: The iliopsoas (iliopectineal) bursa: the largest bursa around the hip, between the iliopsoas tendon and the hip capsule and pubis. It communicates with the hip joint in some people; distension presents as a groin mass and can compress the femoral vessels or nerve.

Subcutaneous trochanteric bursa.description: Bursa between the skin and the greater trochanter, which may become inflamed with direct pressure.

Trochanteric bursa of gluteus maximus mu.description: Large bursa separating the gluteus maximus and iliotibial tract from the greater trochanter. It is traditionally blamed in greater trochanteric pain syndrome, although gluteus medius and minimus tendinopathy is now thought to be the main cause.

Trochanteric bursa of gluteus medius mus.description: Bursa between the tendon of gluteus medius and the greater trochanter, involved in greater trochanteric pain syndrome.

Trochanteric bursa of gluteus minimus mu.description: Bursa between the tendon of gluteus minimus and the anterior surface of the greater trochanter.

Intermuscular gluteal bursae.description: Bursae between the tendon of gluteus maximus and the origin of vastus lateralis near the gluteal tuberosity, reducing friction as the muscle slides over the femur.

Sciatic bursa of gluteus maximus muscle.description: Bursa between gluteus maximus and the ischial tuberosity. Prolonged sitting on hard surfaces inflames it (ischial bursitis, weaver's bottom).

Sciatic bursa of obturator internus.description: Bursa between the obturator internus tendon and the lesser sciatic notch, around which the tendon turns at a right angle as it leaves the pelvis.

Subtendinous bursa of obturator internus.description: Bursa between the tendon of obturator internus and the hip joint capsule.

Bursa of piriformis muscle.description: Bursa between the tendon of piriformis and the upper border of the greater trochanter, near its insertion.

Tendon of extensor digitorum longus.description: Tendons of extensor digitorum longus to the second to fifth toes. They pass under the extensor retinacula in a common synovial sheath, spread over the dorsum of the foot and form dorsal digital expansions on the lesser toes, inserting on the middle and distal phalanges; fibularis tertius runs with them to the fifth metatarsal.

Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris.description: The humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris, arising from the medial epicondyle by the common flexor tendon. It is joined to the ulnar head by a fibrous arch (Osborne's ligament) under which the ulnar nerve enters the forearm - the cubital tunnel, a common site of ulnar nerve entrapment.

Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum su.description: The larger head of flexor digitorum superficialis, arising from the medial epicondyle (common flexor tendon), the ulnar collateral ligament and the coronoid process. The median nerve and ulnar artery pass under the fibrous arch between it and the radial head.

Rectus anterior capitis muscle.description: Rectus capitis anterior: short, flat muscle deep to longus capitis, from the front of the lateral mass of the atlas to the basilar part of the occipital bone in front of the foramen magnum. It flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint and stabilises it.
Rectus anterior capitis muscle.action: Flexes and stabilises the head at the atlanto-occipital joints.

Rectus lateralis capitis muscle.description: Rectus capitis lateralis: short muscle from the upper surface of the transverse process of the atlas to the jugular process of the occipital bone, behind the jugular foramen. It laterally flexes the head and is the counterpart of a posterior intertransverse muscle.
Rectus lateralis capitis muscle.action: Laterally flexes the head to the same side; stabilises the atlanto-occipital joint.
Rectus lateralis capitis muscle.blood_supply: Vertebral, occipital and ascending pharyngeal arteries.

Ventral parts of lateral intertransversa.description: Small muscles between the transverse processes of adjacent lumbar vertebrae (anterior parts of the lateral lumbar intertransversarii). They assist lateral flexion and act mainly as proprioceptive position sensors for the lumbar spine.
innervation: Ventral rami of lumbar spinal nerves
Ventral parts of lateral intertransversa.action: Assist lateral flexion and stabilise adjacent lumbar vertebrae.
